subject: mantisShrimp
pitch:
Category: Animal.
Subject: peacock mantis shrimp.
Style: high-fantasy anime.
reasoning:
I'm planning a TypeScript module depicting a peacock mantis shrimp in a high-fantasy anime style, aiming for a rich but manageable design given I can't test the SDK directly—focusing on its vivid coloring like the green carapace, orange-red legs, and blue antennal scales.

I'm thinking through its anatomy, from segmented body and telson to raptorial claws and swimmerets, deciding to keep the model at roughly real-world scale (~0.18m) while adding fantasy touches like glowing club tips, magical iridescent eye rings, and anime-style hexagonal banding on the stalked compound eyes. I'm also setting up the coordinate system and scale constants to position the body along the z-axis facing forward.

Now I'm working out the rest pose with extended legs and a separate upper/lower jaw structure beneath the head, then planning the skeleton: a thorax root joint with a spine chain running back through the abdomen segments toward the telson, trying to decide the simplest hierarchy of parent-child joints and path points for the tail chain.

For the body itself, I'm considering a swept geometry along the spine chain with an ellipse cross-section for a flat, wide shape, then adding individual tergite plates on top as flattened, colored shapes positioned using frames sampled along the sweep.

I'm also planning the carapace as a separate flattened piece covering the thorax, plus a small rostrum plate up front, both using a green-blue base with orange trim. Now I'm working out the overall front-to-back layout in meters, defining z-positions and widths for the carapace and the wide abdomen section.

Moving on to the tail: the telson forms a wide spiked plate with flanking uropods, and I'm figuring out body height given the legs lift the body off the ground. I'm sketching five pairs of walking legs plus maxillipeds, placing them with two-segment IK bends spreading laterally from the underside down to the ground, and estimating total height including the raised eye stalks.

Now I'm working out the raptorial smashing appendages, folded and extended forward from the head with a bulbous club tip like a peacock mantis shrimp's heel, building each arm as a chain of shoulder, elbow, and club points via a curved path.

For the club itself I'll shape a scaled ellipsoid oriented along the forearm, painted red-orange with a small hook dactyl spike, and add rows of spines along the merus for texture. Now I'm moving on to the eye stalks, rising from the carapace front in an anime-inspired style.

For the eyes, I'm planning large kidney-shaped spheres angled sideways-forward, decaled with a stylized iris showing colored midbands (red, yellow, teal), a sparkle highlight, and surrounding rings to capture that classic anime-eye look on the mantis shrimp's eyestalks.

I'll design the iris with concentric rings — dark green outer, yellow-orange, red, then a black ovoid pupil with white highlights, anime-style with alpha cutting the transparent background so the base shows through.

For antennae, I need the antennules with three flagella plus the characteristic wide, flat antennal scale that mantis shrimp have, along with long whip-like antennae sweeping outward.

Now I'm working out the mouth structure — a small mandible box beneath the rostrum and a lower jaw wedge with teeth, positioned under a head joint that's a child of the thorax, with the raptorial arms emerging around it. I also need to assign rig roles across the skeleton: spine for the thorax root, tail chain, head, jaw, arms, legs, eye stalks as hinges, antennae as tentacles, and uropod fins as a telson fan, all while keeping the total joint count under 160.

Tallying rough joint counts across all these parts puts me around 70 total, which feels manageable. Now I'm setting up the imports for the builder API, deciding whether to pull in a glow kit from a separate module path or just implement emissive material cloning myself to avoid import risk — leaning toward writing my own local glow function for safety.

I'm also thinking through practical details: parts return mesh references, sweeps return mesh arrays, and since the model is tiny I should just work in plain meters rather than scaling awkwardly. For texture resolution I'll stick with the default 1024 atlas size since the total surface area is small enough that it won't need anything larger.

Now I'm picking the color palette for a peacock mantis shrimp with a high-fantasy anime twist—keeping the real creature's emerald carapace, orange-red legs, red club, and blue-green accents but pushing them toward saturated, gem-like tones like emerald, teal, sapphire, crimson, orange, and gold.

I'm also planning subtle magical touches: glowing gold ring bands on the clubs and faint rune decals on the carapace, rendered as a soft glowing texture layered over the shell paint function that blends colors by body region—green dominant on top, teal mixing in toward the underside, and orange-red bands marking segment boundaries along the abdomen.

Now I'm working out the paint logic more precisely—base emerald blending into teal with noise, countershaded belly in orange-cream, and crimson-gold rim lines at each segment edge, using the SDK's color helpers like mix, smoothstep, and rgb.

Next I'm sketching out the joint structure for the body, starting with the thorax joint and building a tail chain using a smooth curve through descending points along the z-axis to shape the abdomen's gentle downward curl.

I'm thinking through how the tail should rest—nearly flat behind the body, with the telson and uropods just above the floor so only the legs truly touch down, keeping everything within that small allowed sink tolerance. Then I'm setting up the tail chain with seven resampled joints parented to the thorax, followed by sweeping the abdomen's shape using a radius function to define its taper.

Adding tergite plates...

I'll add lateral pleura as small flattened cone spikes angled outward-down at ±75° alongside each segment's top plate, giving each of the 8 segments a shell plate plus two side spikes.

I'm also adding dorsal carinae spines -- a small cone at the top-rear center of each plate -- to mimic the longitudinal ridges on a mantis shrimp abdomen.

For plate coloring, I'll paint emerald with an orange rim where the normal's y-component dips low, giving that bold anime-style highlighted edge where the hemisphere plates sink into the body. Next I'm planning the underside swimmerets (pleopods) as paired feathery pads per abdominal segment.

Still shaping the paddle outline...

I'll keep the y value clamped so it doesn't poke below zero, and pull z from the tail's chain point at each position, mirroring x across the two sides using a sign factor.

For the telson and uropods, I'm working out the local coordinate frame at the tail's end so the shield shape with its spiky rear margin sits flat with the correct thickness axis pointing vertically, then extruding an outline that narrows from a wide base toward a rounded tip.

Plotting out marginal spike coordinates...

Mapping out the point sequence...

I'm checking that no edges cross as I trace through the mirrored left half back to the start, and the closing edge looks clean. The telson length of 0.054 seems reasonable at this scale.

Now I'm positioning the telson at the tail end, slightly lowered below the body with a thin beveled edge, attached to the last tail bone joint. For the uropods, I'm planning a pair of two-segment paddles (exopod and endopod) on each side of the telson—oval leaf shapes extending backward with spiky edges, colored orange/blue with red trim, rotated outward at the sides.

Working out the orientation vectors...

Checking the cross product signs for both s=1 and s=-1 cases to verify the mirrored direction consistently points upward, trying a couple of candidate formulas before settling on one that works for both sign cases.

Now I'm sketching the uropod paddle shape as a symmetric leaf-like outline defined by width-vs-length points, planning two paddles per side (an inner endopod and outer exopod) with distinct coloring along the paint direction.

Using smoothing of 1 on the leaf shape should keep corners convex enough to avoid edge-crossing issues, so I'll reuse this generic leaf helper for the antennal scale, swimmerets, and ears too. Now moving to the carapace, building it from a scaled sphere positioned near the body's top with specific radius and scale values.

I'm adding a small forward-pointing rostrum plate near the eyes, working out orthogonal axes for its extrusion direction, then layering in surface detail like a cervical groove, median carina ridge in orange-gold, and lateral spikes near the front corners for a more authentic mantis shrimp carapace shape.

Now I'm thinking about decorative elements on top: maybe a glowing gold rune decal centered on the carapace using an emissive texture map, or alternatively leaning into a peacock motif with teal-and-gold ocellus eyespot decals scattered across the carapace sides and abdomen for a more ornamental look.

Placing ocelli decals on the telson and uropods too, mimicking peacock mantis shrimp coloring in a stylized way, projected onto the curved extruded surfaces. For legs, I'm planning 4-5 visible pairs of pereiopods positioned beneath the thorax.

Still writing leg kinematics...

Each joint aims toward the next in the span, forming the tip joint after three points, and I'm deciding parenting to the thorax works fine for the leg pairs. For the feet, I'm tuning the sweep radius and round cap so the foot rests near the floor at y≈0, and considering adding a small foot pad for extra ground contact.

I'm skipping the flattened ellipse idea and instead placing a tiny cream-colored "toe" sphere at the foot tip so it sits naturally on the ground. Then I'm tapering the leg radius from thicker at the base to thinner near the foot, and painting it orange with a cream gradient toward the tip using a simple height-based color function.

Now I'm mapping out the raptorial arm (the praying mantis-style claw): starting at the shoulder under the carapace front, I'm plotting a forward-down-out path through the elbow joint (merus segment) to the wrist/propodus, ending with a club-shaped dactyl heel around z=0.125, giving the arm a folded-forward resting pose reaching to about z=0.13.

Realizing the total body length is running too long compared to a real mantis shrimp's 15-18cm size, so I'm considering compressing the layout rather than scaling every coordinate, keeping the thorax height fixed and redefining segment lengths to bring the overall body-plus-arm length down to roughly 0.21m total.

Working out the body proportions now: carapace position and size, then the abdomen's seven-joint chain tapering from wider at the front to narrower near the tail.

Adding telson length, eye stalk positions with ellipsoid eyes checked for height, and a rostrum spike between the eyes. Now I'm placing the antennules and starting on the longer second antennae with their scale segments.

Working through arm segment positions — shoulder, elbow, wrist, and club tip — checking the club's radius against floor clearance and whether the arm might clip through the front legs.

Checking the front leg hip placement against the body's underside curve, I'm nudging the joint heights to make sure the legs sit properly beneath the thorax rather than poking inside it.

For the arm skeleton, I'm mapping out a four-point chain—shoulder, elbow, wrist, club—connected through a catmull curve, confirming the span count matches the joint names so the tip resolves correctly at the club.

Working out sweep radii...

Now I'm designing the mantis shrimp club itself: crimson heel with iridescent orange blotches and cream rim as the striking surface, plus a curved dactyl hook and spines along the carpus, and gold ring bands around the club base for detail.

I'm also adding small joint elements like an elbow bulge and a teal/orange joint sphere, then setting up the eye stalk as a two-point chain so the eye attaches as a tip joint.

Everything in the head assembly—eye stalks and eyes—gets parented to the head joint, which itself sits at a forward-aimed offset on the thorax, so the whole cluster moves together. For the eyes themselves I'm shaping a slightly elongated sphere and painting it with a banded UV pattern across the equator to fake a multi-colored compound-eye look.

Now I'm working out the mantis-shrimp-style midband: several narrow rows of distinct colors (yellow, red-orange, cyan) stacked around the eye's equator based on the v-coordinate of the UV mapping. Then I'm adding a small anime-style pupil decal placed near the eye's surface, offset slightly toward the side depending on left/right, sized and lifted just enough to sit visibly on the curved eye without needing mirroring since the texture is symmetric.

Writing SVG eye texture...

Still writing eye SVG...

Now I'm designing the eye pupil with sheen and highlight details, then sketching a peacock-feather ocellus icon with concentric indigo, teal, gold, and sapphire rings, plus a small glowing gold rune sigil for the carapace. I'm also adding mouth and mandible details beneath the head, like a small orange-cream wedge under the rostrum.

Still placing mouth parts...

For fantasy flair, I'm adding a glowing cyan forehead gem, gold filigree trim on the pleura tips, and planning a glowing ocellus accent on the telson.

Now working out the antennal scale geometry and its paint gradient, shaping it to point forward-outward with a teal-to-blue tint and coral-tinted tip.

For the whip antennae, I'm plotting a curved path from the antennal base outward using a Catmull-Rom spline, then sweeping a thin orange tube along it, matching it to the nearest joint since the path points lack bone assignments.

Rather than splitting the tube into 56 banded segments, I'll use a single paint function that alternates orange and cream colors along the sweep parameter, keeping it as one mesh part. Then I'm setting up antennules as a short stalk positioned above the arms and below the eyes, branching into two flagella.

I'm tallying up the total part count across the model: body segments, swimmerets, telson, uropods, carapace, legs, arms, eyes, and antennae roughly add up to around 120 parts, which falls short of the 180-340 target, so I'm considering adding extra detail like carapace texture to pad it out.

Adding more layered details like gold filigree, leg bristles, sternite plates, and telson spikes to push the part count toward 200, then starting to define the builder and the tail chain geometry.

Writing tail chain coordinates...

I'm defining a tapering sweep over the tail chain for the abdomen segments, varying radius per segment with a shell-colored paint and flat end caps.

Now I'm writing the paint function for the shell texture, blending emerald and teal tones based on noise and normal direction, with a lighter belly color where the surface faces downward.

I'm also working out the segmentation for the tail plates—dividing the tail into seven segments along its length, with a dark crimson rim marking each segment boundary, placing plate centers evenly and iterating over them with a sweep callback.

Each plate is a sphere scaled to a flattened shape that tapers slightly along the abdomen's radius, then embedded into the surface by sinking it by a fraction of its own height so it sits naturally against the body.

I'm checking whether the plate's width and curvature stay within the body's elliptical cross-section so the plate doesn't float past the sides—since the plate's height tapers near the edges similarly to the body's surface drop-off, keeping it at 0.9 times the body's radius should keep things visually consistent.

I'm also reconsidering how I'm anchoring the plate vertically: whether the embed fraction should sink the plate's base or its center relative to the body's surface point, since that changes whether the plate reads as resting on the body or partially sunk into it.

That actually forms a nice armored ring, like tergite-pleura-sternite segments, bulging slightly around the body's circumference and tapering to nothing at the disc edges. I want these rings oriented to the chain's local tangent frame so each one wraps the body naturally rather than staying world-axis aligned, scaling them along the radius and thickness accordingly.

For coloring the plates, I'm thinking of using the surface normal to paint gold rim bands where the ellipsoid's front/back normal dominates, giving each ring a metallic edge against a darker body tone elsewhere.

Now I'm adding a dorsal median spike per segment using a cone/spike primitive, placing its base at the sweep's frame point along the normal direction, sized small enough to slightly protrude above the plate surface for a subtle ridge effect.

For the pleural spikes, I'm placing them laterally at roughly ±80 degrees around the segment, using orange-colored cones pointing outward, with the length and radius tuned so they reach just past the body's lateral extent.

Now for the swimmerets, I'm computing their position on the underside of each tail segment by scaling the body's elliptical cross-section, placing them around y ≈ -0.012 to -0.013 depending on lateral offset, then extruding each leaf shape outward along the x-axis from that anchor point.

Let me simplify: define the paddle's local axes with x as the outward-lateral direction and y as the backward-horizontal direction, so the outline forms a flat oval extending outward in x and backward in y.

Still working out the swimmeret orientation vectors...

Now I'm figuring out the telson and uropod positions relative to the tail end, placing two uropods per side with offset direction vectors. I'm also setting up the carapace as a scaled sphere attached to the thorax bone, with a gradient paint scheme shading emerald on top with a lighter highlight.

Writing carapace shader...

Placing a glowing octahedron gem on the forehead, I'm calculating the exact carapace surface height at that point so it sits half-embedded correctly, then adding a thin gold torus bezel around it as a setting.

Now I'm computing a sweep path for a median carina ridge along the top of the carapace, sampling the sphere's surface height at several points from front to back and lifting slightly to create a gold ridge with tapering thickness.

I'm also planning small lateral rostral spikes at the front corners of the carapace, calculating their base position on the ellipsoid surface so they sit flush before extending outward at an angle.

Now I'm setting up the head joint and jaw joint structure with their parent/attachment points and orientation, then defining the upper mandible geometry as a small box shape.

Adding fangs and teeth...

Now for the eye stalks, I'm defining a two-point chain running from a base point near the head up to the eye center, parented to the head with hinge joints so each eye can swivel independently.

Then I'm sweeping the stalk into a thin cylinder with a teal color and flat caps, and placing a small scaled sphere at the tip to form the eye itself, with the eye's joint matching the stalk's tip position.

For extra detail, I'm considering a gold collar ring around the eye's base and a small crescent brow ridge above it, maybe adding tiny orange wedge spikes angled outward for an anime-style eyelash flick, though I might skip some of these flourishes to keep it simple.

Still working out lash placement...

Building the arm chain...

Now I'm defining a tapering radius function for the sweep, thinner toward the tip, and planning the arm coloring as an orange-to-crimson gradient with a lighter belly. I'm also working out where the club head should sit by projecting from the wrist along the arm's direction vector past the tip.

Positioning the club scale and span relative to the computed center point, then sketching the folded dactyl spike as a curved bezier sweep from the club front, colored cream and attached to the club joint bone.

Now I'm defining the club paint: a crimson-to-orange-gold gradient toward the tip with some noise variation, plus a gold torus ring detail near the base attached to the club bone.

Then I'm scattering spines along the dorsal sweep of the club and propodus with outward-facing normals, chaining bone segments. I'm skipping extra dorsal fin blades for now and starting on the walking leg loop, setting up hip and foot coordinates per leg index.

I'm checking whether the leg reach and bend geometry works out — the knee height stays below the body underside and clears the hip-to-foot chord, so the bent-leg proportions look plausible for a short-legged mantis shrimp. Real specimens have stubby legs, so the fit seems reasonable; I may still vary z-offsets slightly per leg for a less uniform stance.

Now I'm setting up foot z-offsets so front legs reach forward and rear legs reach back, then building the leg chain for each side with hip/knee/foot joints plus a contact point for the foot. I'm also cross-checking hip positions along z against the arm shoulder position to make sure the legs and arms don't collide where they're both close together near the thorax.

Then I'm checking leg attachment points against the body's underside curve to confirm the hips sit just inside the surface, deciding to parent all legs to the thorax for simplicity, and setting up the leg sweep geometry with tapered radius and orange/crimson coloring, plus a cream color rule for the lower foot area before adding a toe piece.

Adding the foot sphere now, confirming the leg.tip bone exists for attachment, then sketching bristle spikes along the upper legs across all eight legs. I'm also defining a reusable whip function for antennae using a catmull-rom curve with tapered radii and flat-to-point end caps.

Now I'm working out the orientation of the antennal scale plate, computing its long axis direction and a perpendicular axis via cross product to figure out the thickness vector so the plate sits correctly angled downward.

I'm designing a reusable plate helper function that takes an outline, position, two perpendicular direction vectors, thickness, and color/rim parameters, computing the thickness axis automatically via a vector cross product so I can distinguish face paint from wall paint.

Now I'm working through the telson plate, setting its orientation vectors and dimensions, then adding small ridge spikes along its top surface using a spike helper that takes a base point, direction, length, and radius.

I need to position it carefully at the tail end so it blends smoothly with the abdomen's underside rather than floating above or below it, checking the y-coordinates line up.

Now I'm placing the ocellus decal on the telson, working out the direction and up vectors so it sits symmetrically on the backward-facing plate.

Checking the telson extrude outline coordinates and decal lift height, those seem fine at default. Now working through the eye decal direction vectors - normalizing the side-dependent offset vector for positioning against the eye sphere center.

I'm writing a glow helper that clones a part's material, copies the color into emissive, sets the emissive map, and scales emissive intensity, caching results per material and intensity to avoid duplicate work. Decals confirm they return a Part, and I'm checking how painted parts' materials interact with this caching.

Now I'm weighing whether to add a rune decal on the carapace versus keeping just eye and ocellus glows to stay within the texture budget, and working out the exact position for a gold sigil placed on the carapace top using the surface curvature math.

I'm checking proportions: carapace top around 0.052, abdomen top slightly lower at 0.0455, body roughly 0.037 tall with width 0.052 and length 0.08, giving a suitably chunky mantis shrimp silhouette, and recalculating the median ridge z-values with the updated center offset.

Actually, I'm reconsidering whether the ridge conflicts visually with the rune decal at center — maybe simpler to drop the ridge entirely and instead place a rune at the forehead top, a gem accent, and gold trim sweeps along the carapace sides.

Computing lateral carina positions on the ellipsoid surface...

The draping approach works fine with rough points since nearest-surface projection handles the rest. For the rune decal I need an up vector that isn't parallel to the direction, so [0,0,1] works to orient it facing front. I'll skip ventral sternite detail on the abdomen and move on to defining the color palette constants for the different materials.

Now I'm writing paint functions for each body part -- mixing colors based on position, surface normal, and noise to create gradients and texture variation across the arm and club segments.

For the eye, I'm defining banded color rows based on a vertical UV coordinate, laying out thin stripes of gold, crimson, and cyan to mimic ocelli patterning.

I should be able to import `cells` since it's part of the paint helpers re-exported from the SDK. The sphere's v-coordinate mapping works correctly with three's UV convention (top=1, bottom=0), and the decal placement for the eye over the painted band looks right. Next I'll move on to the head's brow and lashes.

For the tail plates, I'm defining a paint function that classifies ring surfaces by edge versus face normals, blending gold-to-orange at edges and green-to-teal-to-belly-orange gradients across top, sides, and bottom — using world normal direction to decide placement regardless of local frame orientation. I'll apply a similar but darker variant for the abdomen sweep paint.

Now I'm tallying up part counts to check if the model has enough anatomical detail: carapace, eyespots, rune, gem/bezel, carinae, spines, rostrum, jaw with teeth, eyes with stalks/lashes/collars, antennae with flagella, and arm segments with sweep, club, dactyl, ring, and elbow components -- adding up to a fairly dense part list.

Legs, abdomen segments with plates, spikes, pleura, swimmerets, and the telson with uropods bring the total to roughly 160 parts, which seems sufficient, so I'm deciding against adding extra decorative gold rivets, ocelli, or pauldrons to keep things manageable.

Now I'm working through placing ring plates along the tail curve and spikes along the abdomen using position-along-path sampling, with the plate size tapering slightly as it goes, and reasoning through how the frame orientation at each point determines the local axes for scaling the spheroid geometry into a flattened ring shape.

The symmetrical scaling means the up/down orientation of the normal doesn't actually matter for the ring plates, and since the mesh scale applies locally within the frame's rotation, the rigid rings sit correctly on the bending chain while the abdomen stays smooth-skinned. I'm also confirming the ring plates share one material and planning to space seven segments evenly along the tail length.

Checking the ring plate overlap: with segments at 0.0143 each and the plate's half-depth at 0.0085, they'll overlap slightly like shingles, giving a nice banded look with gold edges. For the pleural spikes, the base sits on the body surface while the ring plates extend slightly beyond it, so the spike origin remains valid and should point outward and backward. I'm reconsidering decals for ocelli (eyespots) on the abdomen flanks — since the ring plates protrude more than a typical decal lift, they'd partially hide any decal placed underneath, so I'll skip that approach and think of an alternative.

Writing the leaf outline function...

Defining the plate helper...

Still writing extrude helper...

Checking swimmerets with short length and width for convexity, then setting telson smoothing to zero. For the uropod I'm sizing it with leaf shape and adding two pairs per side at inner/outer angles, now working out placement coordinates.

Fixing the orthogonality math for the direction vectors so the uropod's local axes stay perpendicular and point upward correctly, then applying the same corrected logic to the antennal scale.

I realize the vertical component doesn't break orthogonality since x stays horizontal, so y can droop downward freely while remaining perpendicular to x.

For the antennules, I'm positioning the base and stalk with a bony head shape, then adding two curved flagella whips sweeping to their endpoints, checking they don't badly collide with the rostrum and eyes nearby.

I'm lowering the antennule base and tip so they sit below the eye center, then working out the rostrum leaf's size, orientation, and gold-to-crimson coloring, while computing where the carapace surface sits at that point to position it correctly.

I verify the eye stalk base sits right on the carapace surface at that x,z location, confirming the sqrt calculation matches the expected y value. Then I fix the head joint position and note the jaw placement is fine before moving to decal sizing.
